Ukraine War Thrusts Iran And Turkey Into The Role Of Arms Suppliers
Amir Husain, Forbes, 2022-12-20

The war in Ukraine, which has been raging since February 2022, has thrust two unlikely nations - Iran and Turkey - into the role of key arms exporters. For decades these countries have relied on weapon imports, but now they are looking to turn the tables, leveraging the investments they have made in their domestic industry to emerge as exporters of drones, precision munitions, and more.

As the war continues, Ukraine and Russia seek to rebuild and upgrade their militaries. The conflict thus far has been a major war of attrition, with both sides losing thousands of tanks, dozens of aircraft, and hundreds of helicopters. These massive losses have driven increased demand for arms suppliers, and Iran and Turkey have not hesitated to step into that role. Logistically, the proximity of both countries to the conflict makes them ideal suppliers. In the case of Iran, flights or ships across the Caspian sea allow export to Russia without the need to traverse unfriendly terrain or waters.

Turkey had already made a name for itself internationally as a major exporter of drones. Its Baykar company has received orders for the successful TB-2 attack drone from nearly 20 countries. Ukrainian forces have used this remotely piloted aircraft extensively in the conflict, where it has proved to be a valuable asset.

On the other hand, Iran has filled a major need for Russia by supplying Russian forces with a slow-flying, hard-to-intercept cruise missile, the Shahed. According to some reports, up to 2,000 Shahed-136 drones have been provided to Russia, and a smaller number of reconnaissance unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have also been sold. For Russia, which has expended thousands of its precision-guided standoff weapons, such as Kalibr and Iskander missiles, these drones have helped provide critical capability at a meaningful scale.

Supplying arms to Russia, one of the largest arms producers in the world, is no small achievement and an entirely new role for Iran. While Turkey has already succeeded as an arms exporter, its products have ascended now to legendary status, with Ukrainian citizens composing and singing songs about the TB-2 and its capabilities. The role TB-2 had in the sinking of the Russian Black Sea fleet flagship, "Moskva," and the hundreds of armored vehicles and air defense assets it has so far destroyed have made for a tremendous advertisement in international markets.

Arms sales are becoming a significant source of revenue for both Iran and Turkey, and both countries are likely to continue supplying weapons to all sides of the conflict. Turkey's total defense exports will approach $4B this year, growing at a frenetic 42% yearover-year rate. Meanwhile, Turkey continues to supply weapons to Ukraine while it has maintained a careful balance in its relations with Russia on other matters, such as the procurement of the S-400 air defense system and the brokering of a grain export deal with Russia.

Despite sanctions and the suspension of the JCPOA (Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action), Iran has managed to export weapons to Houthi rebels in Yemen and militias in Iraq and Syria, and it has now added Russia to the list. In exchange, rumors suggest Iran might obtain modern SU-35 multi-role fighters to upgrade its aging airforce. It remains to be seen if Iran will follow up exports of the Shahed drones with larger loitering munitions and even precision ballistic missiles.

The war in Ukraine has had many second and third-order effects on global security. One of these has been the thrusting of Iran and Turkey into the role of major arms suppliers. For both countries, the war serves as an opportunity to increase revenue and gain valuable experience in fielding their indigenously developed weapon systems. The relations Turkey is forging with Ukraine, and Iran with Russia will likely lead to deeper collaboration between them in the future. For example, both Russia and Ukraine are investing in local factories to produce Iranian and Turkish arms domestically.

Based on the success of Turkish products like the TB-2 drone, and Iranian loitering munitions like the Shahed, it is likely that these products - and their sponsoring nations - will see export success elsewhere. And the funds they receive will continue to be reinvested in further developing their arms production capabilities.
